section_summary.extract_value: This discussion section presents the preliminary evaluation of a sociocultural model of mindful eating, focusing on the impact of overhearing family 'fat talk' on mindful eating through positive body image variables. The findings largely supported the hypotheses, showing an inverse association between family fat talk and mindful eating, general body appreciation, and body functionality. Specifically, appreciation for the body's functionality emerged as a significant explanatory mechanism in a college female sample.
section_summary.evidence_source: The present study provided a preliminary evaluation of a sociocultural model of mindful eating grounded in the larger Tripartite Influence Model (Thompson et al., 1999) and supported by research illuminating the specific role of family factors (e.g., parental commentary) in this theoretical framework (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). Specifically, we assessed whether the frequency of overhearing family members complaining about their own physical appearance (i.e., fat talk) negatively predicted mindful eating through two closely-related positive body image variables. Results were mostly in the hypothesized directions. As predicted, overhearing family participate in self-denigrating body commentary was inversely associated with mindful eating, general body appreciation, and specifically appreciating the body's functionality. Additionally, more frequent mindful eating corresponded with higher levels of both positive body image indices. We also found partial support for our initial test of the sociocultural model in predicting mindful eating in the current sample. When considered in concert, only an appreciation for the body's functionality (or body-as-process; Franzoi, 1995) emerged as a significant (albeit modest in size) explanatory mechanism in the link between family fat talk disclosures and overall mindful eating behavior. Overall, our preliminary findings extend earlier tests of family-related influences such as direct parental commentary stemming from sociocultural theory (Thompson et al., 1999) in predicting negative body image and disordered eating (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). We demonstrated that this model featuring the indirect influence of overhearing family fat talk can be successfully applied to accounting for variability in positive body image and mindful eating in a college female sample.
